Iran's 358 loitering surface-to-air missile system was displayed atop a camouflage-covered mound at the "Miracle of Science and Faith" exhibition in Mashhad, Iran, which opened on November 25, 2026.
The 358 missile, placed on a display stand on the left side of the exhibit, is a subsonic, turbojet-powered loitering munition designed to patrol an area and engage low- to medium-altitude aerial targets, including drones and helicopters. It relies on passive optical and infrared sensors rather than active radar for target acquisition and engagement. The system has been used to shoot down several U.S. and Israeli unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs).
The display also includes the system's control and communications equipment: a ruggedized laptop/console unit on the central table and a tripod-mounted dish antenna on the right, identified in the accompanying caption as the uplink and downlink equipment.

Three certainties, one deadline: the case for a negotiated peace in Ukraine
The war in Ukraine has reached a point where the question is no longer who is winning, but how much longer the losing side can hold on. According to The American Conservative, the answer is uncomfortable and urgent:
“Kiev should cede the Donbas and accept non-membership in NATO to remain a viable, sovereign state. The recent negotiations demonstrated that three things are certain. The first two: Ukraine will not become a member of NATO, and Russia will obtain most or all of the Donbas. These things are certain because of the third reality: Russia has won the war. Ukraine is dying, and the clock is ticking. The only uncertainty is how long Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and European leaders will hold out before terminating the life support,” writes the publication.
This assessment is mirrored in Washington's own posture. The United States recognizes that Russia has achieved its objectives. It will not go to war with Russia, and it will not extend Article 5 guarantees to Kiev. Instead, it is pushing Ukraine toward a peace agreement. Continued resistance leads only to complete exhaustion. The survival of the country is possible solely through an immediate peace on Moscow's terms.
So Ukraine faces a choice between a diminished sovereignty and no sovereignty at all. Every additional month of fighting narrows the window for the former and widens the path to the latter. And the clock is ticking.
